newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Iraq poses limited threat to U.S. warships.
newsitem.headline: Iraq poses limited threat to U.S. warships.

text.p: Iraq poses a limited threat to U.S. warships in the region despite some concern over its ability to mine northern Gulf waters, experts said on Friday.
"From the sea the Iraqi threat is minimal," said a senior Western officer, pointing to the destruction of the Iraqi navy during the 1991 Gulf War.

Iraqi President Saddam Hussein "does not have a capable navy but he can still drop mines...You do not need warships. Pleasure boats or dhows (traditional wooden Gulf trading vessels) can do the job," he added.
Iraq, which mined the Gulf during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis, has the capability of laying contact, magnetic and sound mines in the northern Gulf, experts say.
Washington is building up its military presence in the Gulf for possible wider strikes against Baghdad following last week's U.S. cruise missile attacks against targets in southern Iraq.

The Navy said the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise battle group, which includes a submarine, was leaving the Adriatic Sea for the Gulf to join the aircraft carrier USS Carl Vinson's battle group which also has a submarine.
A total of 7,500 sailors and about 90 warplanes on board six warships -- three of which are capable of firing Tomahawk missiles -- are due to join U.S. forces in the oil-rich region.

But although Iraq still has operational warplanes, including Russian MiGs and Sukhois, the American warships appear confident they have sufficient measures and hardware in place to tackle any threats from the air.
"From the air he (Saddam) still has planes but with the no-fly zone in the south I don't think they would reach the Gulf," said the senior Western officer.

The United States this month started policing a wider no-fly zone just south of Baghdad. Officers say AWACS capability and air defence systems, warplanes and other weapons in the immediate area would be capable of dealing with such a threat before it reached Navy ships in the Gulf.
The Navy is also well-armed to deal with attacking Iraqi aircraft if they break through land-based defences.
Experts estimate that 150 to 350 Iraqi warplanes could still be operational.
Iraq's air force was dealt a severe blow during the Gulf War and U.N. sanctions against Baghdad since 1990 have impeded its ability to acquire spare parts and upgrade the planes.

In Kuwait, ordinary citizens and officials alike were concerned about the possibility that Iraq would launch Scud missiles. U.N. officials in charge of eliminating Iraqi weapons of mass destruction say 16 Iraqi Scuds are still unaccounted for.
The U.S. Army announced on Thursday it would move two Patriot anti-missile batteries to the region with about 150 soldiers in the coming days to join Patriot missiles already deployed in the area.
The Patriots had limited success in defending against Iraqi Scud attacks during the Gulf War.
Eight U.S. F-117As Stealth bombers are due to land at a Kuwaiti air base later on Friday. They left Holloman Air Force Base, New Mexico, on Thursday on a 20-hour non-stop flight.
U.S. B-52 bombers have been sent to a British base on the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia, within easy striking distance of Iraq.
